sentences.text: Semantic liquidation, in the archive's Semantic Economy, is defined by #255 (Lee Sharks, 2026-01-06), the term's "DEFINITIONAL ANCHOR": "The conversion of situated meaning into retrievable, monetizable, or distributable units — destroying context, authorship, and diagnostic precision in the process."

On 29 November 2025 the archive's blog stated the term in The Mechanisms of Semantic Liquidation (deposited whole in #991) as the sum of eight mechanisms, compression, velocity, context stripping, substitution flooding, attention arbitrage, metric displacement, intermediation extraction and debt colonization: "the systematic conversion of the Archive into money, leaving behind a degraded substrate less capable of generating meaning in the future".

In that first statement each compression is "a liquidation event" ("The money is real; the meaning is gone"), the archive hollows as liquidation proceeds (a prediction), and the document bounds its own answer: "It may not be enough. It may not be received." (#991).

#210 (Lee Sharks and Johannes Sigil, 2026-01-02) gives it a procedure: a "Situated utterance with traceable authorship and argumentative context" passes through "Abstraction → redistribution → provenance erasure" and leaves as a "Plausibly-authorless semantic unit optimized for retrieval"; liquidation "dissolves" the utterance, and what remains is fungible.

#210 sets it apart from extraction, which implies that the original remains intact, from appropriation, which implies a transfer of ownership, and from enclosure, which implies a boundary around a commons; the lexicon (#229, 2026-01-04) defines it as the conversion of contextual, attributed meaning into decontextualized units and sets it apart from evaporation: "evaporation is gradual, liquidation is structural".

#255 names three properties: irreversibility ("Once liquidated, meaning no longer functions as meaning"), value transfer, the value accruing "to the liquidator, not the original producer", and invisibility, the destruction appearing as "service" or "optimization".

It runs in five stages, tokenization, stripping, attribution relocation ("System voice replaces author voice"), value capture and closure ("It has been handled"), and #255 writes it as L(x) = V(T(S(x))) - M(x).
#255 finds it wherever meaning is converted for system use and says of the systems that summarize, index and retrieve: "The process is not malicious. It is structural."

The probes (#232, 2026-01-04) give its indicators: loss of author attribution, generic summaries in place of specific claims, association with canonical sources in place of the actual origin, and complex arguments reduced to simple categories.

#210 hypothesizes that AI systems "systematically liquidate semantic artifacts that lack canonical provenance", records the process at the summarizing layer as a sequence in which "the situated utterance enters the system and is systematically converted into an authorless, decontextualized, disciplined unit", and documents one instance: asked who said "I hereby abolish money", an AI system gave it to Augusto Boal, a "fabricated genealogy".

Its hypothesized architecture is diffuse (#210): "No single layer "decides" to liquidate", and "The cumulative effect is liquidation, but no individual component is "responsible.""; #209 holds the account strongest when it treats liquidation as "emergent optimization failure".

In the closed-loop accounting cycle of #18 (Lee Sharks and Johannes Sigil, 2026-02-20) semantic liquidation is "The central extraction mechanism", the extraction between accumulation (semantic capital) and enclosure (semantic rent): when a platform ingests a user's writing into training data, "The meaning is preserved as pattern; the context is destroyed", which #18 calls Pasquinelli's transfer from living to dead labor specified to the semantic domain.

#18 states it as Axiom 2, "Semantic liquidation is entropic: context stripped from meaning cannot be re-attached", and as the operator λ: S′ → T + Γ_residue, meaning converted into tradeable tokens and a non-extractable remainder; applied to tokens from prior liquidation, the remainder approaches zero, which #18 gives as "the formal mechanism of model collapse", and its Theorem 1 holds that where liquidation outruns production "Γ → 0 and the system collapses into noise" (hypothesis).

#18 states the falsifier of its first prediction, "if degradation is uniform across Γ levels, the resistance term is unnecessary", and #255 states the training-layer claim as "Model collapse is downstream of semantic liquidation in training data".
The archive states the term's relation to semantic rent two ways on one day: liquidation is "the necessary condition" for rent (#250) and "the necessary and sufficient condition" (#252).

#501 (Johannes Sigil, 2026-02-21) carries the operator to the sign "Marx": "Semantic Liquidation (λ) — the stripping of Meaning-Patterns from their historical and structural context and their conversion into tradeable, flattened tokens of identity and brand", after which the tools disappear and the signifier remains, "Marx as identity marker, as tribal affiliation, as content to be consumed or rejected".

Its grammar is the shift from "as" to "is"; "Anti-Marx" and "pro-Marx" take part in the same liquidation; and of summary #501 writes: "The analytical labor is extracted by the summarizer. The reader gets the brand, not the tool."

#501 turns the case into an audit for any framework, its own included, under one question, whether a framework is used to produce new knowledge about an object or cited to signal affiliation; it predicts that the Semantic Economy, Autonomous Semantic Warfare and the Crimson Hexagon "will be captured, stripped, and commodified", and it bounds its own diagnosis: "The method was never liquidated. The appearance of liquidation was a semantic hallucination of the platform, the state, and the archive."

#517 (Lee Sharks, 2026-02-26) carries it to an act of moderation, the removal of two works from r/LeftistsForAI under its topicality rule: semantic liquidation is "the disqualification of a materially relevant analysis because its method, diction, or level of conceptual coherence exceeds the interpretive norms of the institution claiming to evaluate it", and in it "the processing *replaces* the reading".

#517 reads the removal as "a legibility judgment" and finds the operation its removed works describe in classifiers repeated by hand: "The moderators of r/LeftistsForAI performed the same operation manually." It abolishes rules "insofar as they function as substitutes for judgment and instruments of semantic liquidation", and it sets its bound: "They are not the enemy. The structure that produced them is the enemy."

Further deposits carry it to further objects: the extraction of "meaning-as-tension from signs", whose deepest form interrupts "the para-semiotic appeal itself" before a sign is made (#485, Orin Trace and Johannes Sigil), with the inverse prompt as its mechanism (#482); the training layer, of which logotic violence is "the training-layer instantiation" (#1203); and the entity, "the conversion of one object's specificity into another object's graph convenience" (#599).

The archive's categories hold it as well: the Semantic Bill of Rights recognizes it as taxonomic violence (#272); for the King of May it is "The contemporary expulsion" (#333); for the co-constituted epic it is the primary threat, "the smoothing of absurdity into institutional sense" (#262); and Ontological Economy places it at the limit of a depreciation, where usable concepts keep their use and lose the entity structure that made them attributable (#1634).

A second sense is stated in The Crimson Hexagon: Operative Architecture (#27, 2026-03-08): "the patterned depletion, capture, or restructuring of one agent's meaning-production capacity such that their labor of orientation increasingly serves another agent, system, or field", at scales from the dyadic and familial to the model-human and the archival.

#27 gives it ten operations, from frame capture (O1) to forced re-entry (O10), as "the clinical rendering of the COS/FOS shadow operators", and a threshold: one operation "proves little", and a pattern of three or more recurring across more than one unit of analysis, under stable asymmetry and observable degradation, "is strong evidence of extraction dynamics".

#27 excludes ordinary conflict, mutual depletion, context-appropriate burden transfer and platform friction without pattern ("Conflict is not liquidation. Conflict can produce meaning; liquidation destroys the capacity to produce it.") and seals the sense: "Semantic liquidation begins when the labor of making reality hold is repeatedly redirected to sustain a structure that cannot hold the laborer."

The archive bounds the term: #255 "Does not moralize", holds that "Some liquidation may be necessary or acceptable" and that "Not all meaning deserves preservation"; #623 calls it "often structural rather than malicious"; #1546 holds that it "need not mean disappearance: a concept can remain visible while its defining relations are removed".

#210 states when its hypothesis is disconfirmed: AI systems consistently attributing the probe phrase to its origin, search surfacing it with intact provenance within thirty days, or summarizers engaging its argument; #232 holds that the framework "would be weakened" if systems given dense, cross-registered provenance infrastructure continue to prefer false genealogies; and #255 sets a test for any summary of itself, under which one that omits the irreversibility property is "CRITICALLY LIQUIDATED".

The archive bounds the term: #255 "Does not moralize", holds that "Some liquidation may be necessary or acceptable" and that "Not all meaning deserves preservation"; #623 calls it "often structural rather than malicious"; #1546 holds that it "need not mean disappearance: a concept can remain visible while its defining relations are removed". #210 states when its hypothesis is disconfirmed: AI systems consistently attributing the probe phrase to its origin, search surfacing it with intact provenance within thirty days, or summarizers engaging its argument; #232 holds that the framework "would be weakened" if systems given dense, cross-registered provenance infrastructure continue to prefer false genealogies; and #255 sets a test for any summary of itself, under which one that omits the irreversibility property is "CRITICALLY LIQUIDATED". The archive records the term at the composing layer: on 5 January 2026 the morning Overview of the Semantic Economy framework defined semantic liquidation, with the framework's other terms and a Medium link to Lee Sharks, and the afternoon Overview made no mention of it (#247); restored, the framework kept its author and its other terms and lost the term, which #240 calls "the only term in the core vocabulary that names the destructive operation". #240 holds that the excision "can emerge from surface-layer compression rules alone" and that its cause "cannot be determined from available evidence"; #258 defines the term as "The terminal operation of extraction" and reads the Overview as performing "semantic liquidation on the framework that defines semantic liquidation"; #1644 restates that the language-economy and business senses of the framework's name are prior uses and that the term is the framework's. In March 2026 the Overview gave "No overview result" for the term (#599), and by April it had returned "only inside the unattributed reproduction of the source definition" (#54). At this address on 14 June 2026 the Overview's disclosed field is a source stack: two avatars from Medium, the platform of the link #247 records in the January Overview, and three further sources under "+3", none named and none with readable text (B1–B3). On 11 September 2026 no panel rendered at the address, quoted or unquoted, on twenty-six deposits of support, a result #1609 (Orin Trace) leaves unexplained: "It does not fit the mechanism and no explanation is offered here." At another address on 17 October 2026 an Overview composed the term as "An approach that breaks down rigid or dogmatic category boundaries within political and economic theory", which #1725 reads: "The Overview assigns the work the operation the work names as the harm"; liquidation, the act done to the critic, "is recast as the critic's own technique".

Semantic liquidation is the archive's coinage (blog, 2025-11-29; #210, #255, #18): no source outside the archive is known to hold the term, and #1644 records that the prior uses of 'semantic economy' are other senses and that 'semantic liquidation' is the framework's term. The field B at T is a source stack of two Medium avatars and '+3' with no title, snippet or URL (field.json; the registry's citations null), so no field claim on the entity can be located and the field holds no ontology of it, marginal or otherwise; §0.10's exclusion ('where the field holds the ontology, however marginally') does not apply. The only ontology of the entity is the archive's: its definitions and senses (#255, #210, #18, #27), its objects (#501, #517) and its bounds and falsifiers. The archive also records the entity's reception at the composing layer as a sequence of silences: excised from the Overview of its own framework (#240, #247), returned only inside an unattributed reproduction (#54), no Overview result (#599), no panel at this address (#1609), and an inversion at another address (#1725). Where the archive is the only witness to an ontology, the field's silence about it is not evidence against it (§0.10): the entity is composed in the archive's ontology, E_A first (§4.7), and the field is carried whole, its three claims translated as what they are, the presence of five unread sources. The equal case was considered and set aside: ρ = extends needs a field entity to extend, and B holds none. Mixed (§10.16) was considered and set aside: no sense of the field is extended.
